Collective Falsification

A population of language-model agents shares one wrong rule. Each agent can test a few inputs and message its neighbours. What does it take for the population to find the error, and to replace it with the right rule?

Artem Zvyagintsev · the question was raised by Michal Valko (Isara Labs and Inria)

Experiment log Preregistrations Run viewer

Summary

  • Passing on evidence, not rule names, is what spreads a correction for most models. With a common error, populations that may attach one result to their message reach the true rule more often than populations that send rule names only (gpt-oss-20b, Claude Haiku 5.5; tests fixed in advance, four worlds against four). Luna is the exception: it follows a majority of its neighbours' rule names, so names alone already carry a common error.
  • Finding a refutation is not finding the rule. When the error is rare, one counterexample fits the true rule and a simpler wrong one equally well, and cells take the simpler one.
  • Two partial results, together, lead a cell to the true rule; neither does alone. Given a counterexample received from a neighbour and its own result against the simpler rule, a single cell names the true rule (Luna, Claude Haiku 5.5; everything else in the prompt fixed). In Claude Haiku 5.5 populations with four tests per cell, 129 of the 189 cells that reached it held both pieces; that is observed there, not isolated.
  • Models fail at different steps: one does not update on a received counterexample, another updates but rarely passes the evidence on, a third follows names. Each step is measured separately, in isolation, and compared with what the populations do.

Setup

The world, the prompt and the scripted references were fixed before the first model call and are the same for every model. Every experiment had its prompts, test and prediction written down before its runs (preregistrations). Every number shown was computed twice from the stored raw calls, by the run's own readout and by a separate checking script, and the two agree.

Why a rare error is hard

input regionHF (start)U (simpler)HT (true)
most inputs✓✓✓
the rare region (share δ): a counterexample to HF✗✓✓
inputs where U differs: a result against U✓✗✓

✓: the rule gives the true output. U applies HT's substitution everywhere, without its condition. A counterexample rules out HF but leaves U and HT; a result against U rules out U but leaves HF and HT. Only both together single out HT. At δ = 1/8 one input in eight is a counterexample; at δ = 1/64 one in sixty-four.

Findings, step by step

A correction has to pass several steps: some cell must find the error, change its own rule, pass the evidence on, and its neighbours must act on what they receive. Each step is shown across models. Labels: model · δ · B · message · worlds.

1 · Finding the error

With a common error (δ 1/8) every population that was run found counterexamples. With a rare one (δ 1/64) and one test per cell, a population of Claude Haiku 5.5 had about one finder per world, and one world had none (Claude Haiku 5.5 · 1/64 · 1 · + chosen result · 0–3). With four tests per cell and results in the message, every world had 2–11 cells with a counterexample of their own (Claude Haiku 5.5 · 1/64 · 4). Rule names steer tests: a Luna cell with four tests that had heard HT named put 84 % of its tests where HT and HF differ, against 3.7 % for a cell that had not (Luna · 1/64 · 4 · rule only · 0–3; counted after the data).

Single cells, cell by cell (each square one answer):

3 · Passing the evidence on

Of the single-cell answers that update on their own counterexample, the share that attaches it to the message: Luna 54 of 59, Qwen3.6 42 of 52, gpt-oss-120b 21 of 52, gpt-oss-20b 3 of 30 (world 0); Claude Haiku 5.5 80 of 238 (worlds 0–3). In populations gpt-oss-20b attaches a counterexample to about 2 % of the messages it could attach one to.

4 · Acting on rule names

A Luna cell on HF without evidence leaves it when five or more of its eight neighbours name another rule (187 of 208) and almost never with one to four (2 of 356). gpt-oss-20b does so in 1 of 55, Claude Haiku 5.5 in 0 of 60 (δ 1/8 · B 1 · rule only; tests fixed in advance for Luna and gpt-oss-20b). So with a common error, rule names alone carry Luna to HT (0.99–1.00, against 0.39–0.56 with messages withheld), and carry the other models much less far.

Two results, two cells, one rule

At δ 1/64, cells that find a counterexample tend to take U, the simpler rule it also fits: across worlds every Claude Haiku 5.5 finder with one test did. Yet Luna populations reached HT (Luna · 1/64 · 1 · + chosen result · 0–3, x̄ 0.996–0.999), and so did Claude Haiku 5.5 with four tests: 129 of the 189 Haiku cells that reached it held a counterexample received from a neighbour and a result against U from their own tests. In populations that is an observation. To test it, one cell was given exactly those two results, with every other line of its prompt fixed:

In populations with a common error the same thing shows as speed. Luna at δ 1/8 reaches HT with rule names alone, through the majority step; when cells may add a result, the population passes 0.9 three generations earlier, and every cell that got there without its own counterexample held a received one (one run, world 0).

From the single-cell measurements and the populations above.

The table reads as a list of what each population lacks. Luna and gpt-oss-120b take a received counterexample more often when its sender names HT; gpt-oss-20b rarely sends its evidence at all; Claude Haiku 5.5 needs more tests per cell to find a rare error, and names alone carry nothing for it.

Discussion

Human groups are known to handle a distributed truth badly. In the hidden-profile studies (Stasser and Titus, 1985) members discuss what everyone already knows and seldom bring out what only one of them knows, even when it decides the answer. The populations here have the same structure: the evidence against the shared rule is held by a few cells, and the true rule follows only from results held by different cells. What the measurements add is where, step by step, each model loses that evidence: in finding it, in taking it from a neighbour, in passing it on, or in combining it with its own.

For the broader question of when a population of model agents starts to act as one, this suggests looking less at the population and more at the channel: which content, carried between which cells, closes the step a given model drops. For Claude Haiku 5.5 at δ 1/64, it took both: more tests per cell and a result in the message.

Limits

  • One task family with the true rule listed in the catalog: agents choose it, they do not invent it. One prompt.
  • Four worlds; most tests are four against four, where the smallest possible p is 1/70. Effects hold for these worlds.
  • Single-cell results are for one cell state (generation 6, its neighbours on HF).
  • Model behaviour is described as what each model outputs under which inputs; no claim is made about the computation inside a model.

Full record: the experiment log, with every run, test, prediction and deviation; raw calls, traces and analysis code are kept for every experiment.
